# Cross-Model Analysis and Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The model sections of @sec-results compare the harnesses one model at a time. Placed side by side, the four models show which differences belong to a harness and which arise only from its combination with a particular model. On every model, the harness changed how many tasks were solved and what the same work cost, but rarely in the same direction twice. What recurred were properties of the harnesses themselves: how they keep their context and cache, how they handle commands that do not finish, and how well their tool interface suits the model they run.

## Task success across models

On every model, the best and the weakest harness were three to five of the ten tasks apart. Which harness was which, however, changed from model to model.

### No harness is best on every model

@fig-cross-success orders the models by their median cost per task and joins the results of each harness. The lines cross, and every harness that leads on one model falls behind on another. A ranking of harnesses measured with one model therefore says little about the next.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-success
#| fig-cap: "Tasks passed per harness and model, with the models ordered by their median cost per task. The green band marks the best result on a model or one task behind it; the shaded column marks the model with only two harnesses. Grey: DeepSWE's reference harness `mini-swe-agent` on the same tasks and models, as the mean of its four rollouts per task; the bar shows the range in which two of three single runs would fall, estimated from these rollouts. DeepSWE has no rollouts of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash."

plot_success_by_model(cross);
```

The model sections show why the positions change: a harness feature turned into an advantage or a handicap only through the way a model used it. Claude Code's weakest result, on GPT-5.6 Luna, coincided with the only extensive delegation in the benchmark; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3 started no subagent in any harness, and GLM-5.3-Flash started two (@sec-luna-delegation; @sec-glm-context). Codex's weakest result, on GLM-5.3-Flash, came with almost a quarter of its edits rejected, under a profile derived from a GPT model (@sec-glm-tools). Pi lost one trial each on Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3-Flash to a shell command that never returned (@sec-kimi-success; @sec-glm-success). Delegation, a scripted edit interface, and a shell without a time limit are neither good nor bad in themselves. They cost tasks only with a model that used them in a particular way.

Many of the remaining differences hinge on single tests. Of the 57 failed trials with a test result, 44 passed at least 90% of their fail-to-pass tests, so whether a trial counts as solved often depends on one or two tests. DeepSWE's four `mini-swe-agent` rollouts per task show how much such outcomes vary between runs [@deepsweTrials2026]: taking one rollout per task, a ten-task run of the same model varies by 1.3 to 1.4 tasks (one standard deviation), which the grey bars show. A difference of one or two tasks between two harnesses therefore lies within the variation of repeated runs. The gaps of four and five tasks between the best and the weakest harness on GPT-5.6 Luna, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Kimi K3 are larger than two independent runs would typically differ.

The same reference shows what a minimal harness achieves. `mini-swe-agent` gives the model a shell and nothing else, and only on GLM-5.3-Flash did three of the four full harnesses clearly exceed it. On GPT-5.6 Luna and Kimi K3, the best harness stayed within the minimal agent's range, and the others reached its lower edge or fell below it. Dedicated read, edit, and search tools, context management, and delegation therefore did not reliably solve more tasks than a shell alone. Compaction, the only context feature that came into play, did so only on GPT-5.6 Luna. There, Codex used OpenAI's server-side compaction, yet OpenCode V2 passed two tasks more with plain-text summaries written by the model (@sec-luna-context). The weakest results above coincided with a feature that a model used badly or with a missing safeguard, not with a lack of tools. The reference ran on other provider routes than this study, so the comparison is indicative.

### OpenCode V2 as the consistent harness

Against this background, OpenCode V2 stands out because its position changed least. It is the only harness inside the green band on every model it ran on (@fig-cross-success). Its seven passed tasks were a different set on each model, and only 5 tasks were passed on all three. Its consistency therefore lies in how many tasks it solved, not in a fixed set of tasks it always solves, and single runs cannot show whether it would persist over repeated runs.

The tasks that only one harness solved, or only one failed, show where the harnesses differ most. @fig-cross-exclusive collects them for the three models with all four harnesses and weights each by how rarely DeepSWE's reference runs solved the task, so that solving a hard task counts more than failing an easy one [@huang2026deepswe]. OpenCode V2 is the only harness with a net gain, and one of its exclusive solves is the hardest task of the set. Codex and Pi solved no task that all other harnesses failed. The weights describe the tasks in general rather than for a particular model, and a repeated run could move any block, so the figure shows a tendency rather than a ranking.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-exclusive
#| fig-cap: "Tasks that only one harness solved (right) or only one harness failed (left), on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna, and GLM-5.3-Flash. Block width is 1 minus the task's DeepSWE solve rate for a solve and the solve rate for a failure; the percentage in each block is the solve rate. The net value is the difference of both sides."

plot_exclusive_outcomes(cross);
```

OpenCode V2 reached these results with a handicap. Its native `grep` and `glob` tools failed in every call, because they depend on a ripgrep binary that the sandbox could not download (@sec-opencode-ripgrep). 29 of its 30 trials called them, 102 times in total, and then fell back to shell commands. A tool that fails can only cost calls, so where the search tools work, OpenCode V2 can be expected to perform at least as well. How much a working search would add was not measured.

## Cost of the same tasks in different harnesses

A harness does not change the price of a token, but it decides how many tokens a task consumes and how many of them the provider serves from its cache. Because all harnesses of a model ran the same ten tasks, these effects can be compared directly, apart from the price level of the model.

### Cost against success

@fig-cross-cost-success places every model--harness combination by the tasks it passed and by the normalized cost of the ten tasks. The price of the model decides where on the cost axis a group of harnesses lies; within the group, the harness decides how much the same ten tasks cost. Apart from Claude Code on GPT-5.6 Luna, the most expensive harness of a model cost up to about twice as much as the cheapest. On single tasks, the harnesses of a model differed by a median factor of 1.4 to 1.8 between the cheapest and the most expensive. Claude Code on GPT-5.6 Luna is the exception by an order of magnitude: its delegation multiplied the tokens of every task, and it solved fewer tasks than any other harness on that model (@sec-luna-delegation).

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-cost-success
#| fig-cap: "Tasks passed against the normalized cost of the ten tasks for every model--harness combination; the label names the model, and the cost axis is logarithmic. Kimi K3 ran only in Codex and Pi. A marker that would overlap another is shifted to the right by at most 3% of its cost. The green band marks 7 and 8 passed tasks, the best result on every model or one task behind it."

plot_cost_success(cross);
```

Cost and success did not go together. The cheapest harness of a model passed between two and seven tasks, the most expensive one between three and eight. OpenCode V2 is the only harness that ran at or near the lowest cost of each of its models and stayed in the green band at the same time. No other harness passed as many tasks for less, and per passed task, it was the cheapest harness on all three of its models. It did not reach the best result everywhere, however. On DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, Claude Code passed one task more, for 28% and 23% more than OpenCode V2 on the same tasks, and it was the most expensive harness on all three of its models. Between these two harnesses, the choice is therefore one of one more solved task against a lower cost.

Which harness is cheaper also depends on how the model's tokens are priced. Output tokens made up between 4% and 33% of a harness's cost; the rest is input, most of it history that every step resends. On DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, a cached input token costs 2% of an uncached one, so the few uncached tokens decide the cost. Claude Code and Pi used the fewest input tokens there, but cost more than Codex and OpenCode V2 because they read a smaller share of them from the cache (@sec-deepseek-cost). On GLM-5.3-Flash, a cached token costs a fifth of an uncached one, and the volume weighs more: Codex, with the fewest input tokens, was the cheapest harness in total (@sec-glm-cost). The same difference between two harnesses thus costs more or less depending on the model's price list, and a cost ranking of harnesses measured with one model does not transfer to another.

A lean harness does not lead to lower token use either. @fig-cross-prompt compares the harness's own prompt, the system prompt and tool definitions that are sent with every request, with the tokens used per task. The prompts differ ninefold, but the tokens per task do not follow them. Pi, with the smallest prompt, used about as many tokens as the other harnesses, and more than Claude Code once Kimi K3 is left out. The fixed prompt is a small part of every request, and the history that builds up while the model works dominates the token use. What a harness costs therefore depends on how long its sessions run and how much of their history the cache covers, not on the size of its own prompt.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-prompt
#| fig-cap: "(a) Prompt tokens of each trial's first request, which contains the system prompt, the tool definitions, and the task; median over the models. (b) Input and output tokens per task; median over the models. The hatched extensions show the value without Kimi K3, the only model with two harnesses."

plot_prompt_and_tokens(cross);
```

### Cache use

Because most input tokens are resent history, the share read from the cache largely decides what they cost (@sec-cost-accounting). OpenCode V2 kept the highest or nearly the highest share on every model (@fig-cross-cache). On GLM-5.3-Flash, the other three harnesses fell several points below their level on the other models, whereas OpenCode V2 did not. The trajectories do not show why.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-cache
#| fig-cap: "Share of the input tokens read from the cache per harness and model. The hollow diamond shows Claude Code's root session on GPT-5.6 Luna without its subagents."

plot_cache_share(cross);
```

What lowers the share is visible on GPT-5.6 Luna. Claude Code's subagents each started with a new context, and its root session alone reached a share close to that of the other harnesses. The first OpenCode V2 run, which compacted in every trial, read clearly less from the cache than the rerun (@sec-luna-compaction). Delegation and compaction both replace the shared beginning of consecutive requests, which is what the cache reuses [@gim2024promptcache]. The cache share thus reflects how a harness manages its context. Since every response reports its cached tokens, it can be monitored without additional tooling.

### Spending on failed trials

A failed trial is paid in full, so the tokens a harness spends before it stops are part of its cost. @fig-cross-lost-tokens divides the tokens of each model--harness combination into those spent in passed and in failed trials and marks the share of trials that passed. Where the solid part ends above the mark, the failed trials used fewer tokens than their share of the trials. This holds for almost every combination; only Pi on GPT-5.6 Luna and on Kimi K3 spent more than that share on its failures. The large failed share of Claude Code on GPT-5.6 Luna follows from its seven failed tasks, not from failures that were larger than its solutions; its problem is the total volume of every trial. No harness therefore spent a disproportionate part of its tokens on the tasks it failed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-lost-tokens
#| fig-cap: "Share of the input and output tokens of each model--harness combination spent in passed trials (solid) and in failed trials (hatched). The black mark shows the share of trials passed, where the solid part would end if every trial had used the same number of tokens; below each bar are the passed trials. The number above each bar is the mean number of tokens per task."

plot_lost_tokens(cross);
```

Tasks differ in size, so these shares do not show whether a harness overspent on a particular task. That shows when each failed trial is compared with the passing trials of the other harnesses on the same model and task (@fig-cross-failure-cost). Only Claude Code's failures cost clearly more than a solution, typically 5.44 times as much, and these come from GPT-5.6 Luna. OpenCode V2's failures cost less than a solution, and Codex's about as much. Pi's failures appear cheap only because of Kimi K3; without it, they cost about as much as a solution. Apart from Claude Code on GPT-5.6 Luna, no harness turned a task it could not solve into an exceptional cost. With five to fifteen comparable failures per harness, these values describe tendencies.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-failure-cost
#| fig-cap: "Cost of each failed trial relative to the median cost of the passing trials on the same model and task, only for tasks that at least one harness passed. The bar under each row marks the typical value, the geometric mean over all models; the hatched part shows how it shifts without Kimi K3. Hollow dots are Kimi K3 failures. The axis is logarithmic."

plot_failure_cost(cross);
```

## Tool interfaces and safeguards

The tools of a harness decide how much a model can do in one step and what happens when a step does not end. Codex's JavaScript tool and Pi's shell without a time limit affected several models in this way.

### Codex's JavaScript tool

Codex has no separate read or edit tool. The model writes JavaScript cells that call shell and patch functions (@sec-luna-tools), so a single cell could combine several actions. @fig-cross-actions shows that the models rarely did this: most Codex cells contain one tool call, and on three of the four models, the other harnesses combined several actions in one step more often through ordinary parallel tool calls. The flexibility therefore saved neither agent steps nor tokens. Apart from Claude Code on GPT-5.6 Luna, which took a median of 666 steps in its root session and 2,787 with its subagents, all harnesses needed similar numbers of steps.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-actions
#| fig-cap: "Share of agent steps with more than one tool call. For Codex, a step is one JavaScript cell, counted when it calls more than one tool function; for the other harnesses, a step with several parallel tool calls."

plot_actions_per_step(cross);
```

The flexibility did bring errors. @fig-cross-errors shows Codex with the highest share of rejected tool calls on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Kimi K3. On Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3-Flash, most of these rejections were JavaScript errors in the cell itself or patches that `apply_patch` rejected (@sec-kimi-tools; @sec-glm-tools). Only on GPT-5.6 Luna, the one model with a native Codex profile (@sec-methodology), are Codex's rejections comparable to those of the other harnesses; the three other models ran with a profile derived from GPT-5.6 Sol. The interface thus works with the model family it was built for and costs errors with the others.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-errors
#| fig-cap: "Share of tool calls rejected as invalid invocations, counted as in the model sections. The hollow diamond shows Claude Code's root session on GPT-5.6 Luna without its subagents."

plot_invocation_errors(cross);
```

### Long-running commands

A command that does not finish, such as a server or a program stuck in a loop, stalls an agent unless the harness stops it or returns control to the model. @tbl-cross-safeguards compares how the harnesses handle this. Pi alone has neither a background mode nor a default time limit: its shell tool stops a command only if the model passes a timeout [@pi0844BashTool].

| Harness | Background execution | Default limit per command | Observed in the trials |
|:--------|:---------------------|:--------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Claude Code | `run_in_background`, with tools to read or stop the output | 2 minutes [@claudeCodeToolsReference] | 35 background commands; 6 commands stopped at 2 minutes |
| Codex | Commands keep running in a session | None; control returns after a set wait | Up to 23 consecutive checks of a running command |
| OpenCode V2 | `background` parameter | 2 minutes for foreground commands [@opencode208ShellTool] | 23 background commands; no command reached the default limit |
| Pi | None | None | 2 trials hung until the time limit |

: Handling of long-running shell commands in the canonical trials. {#tbl-cross-safeguards tbl-colwidths="[16,32,22,30]"}

Whether the missing limit matters depends on the model (@fig-cross-pi-timeouts). GPT-5.6 Luna set a timeout on almost every Pi shell call, the other models on about one in six. Both Pi trials that hung ran with such models: on Kimi K3 and on GLM-5.3-Flash, a shell command never returned, and each trial waited until the three-hour limit (@sec-kimi-success; @sec-glm-success). An interactive user would notice such a stall and interrupt it. In unattended use, such as the benchmark or an automated pipeline, the agent waits for hours without progress. The missing safeguard is a property of the harness; the model's habits decide how often it takes effect.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cross-pi-timeouts
#| fig-cap: "Share of Pi's shell calls in which the model set a timeout itself, and the Pi trials that reached the three-hour time limit because a command never returned."

plot_pi_timeouts(cross);
```

## Lost reasoning in the gateway {#sec-discussion-reasoning-loss}

The largest effect on task success and cost in this study came not from a harness but from the gateway between the harnesses and the models. Defects in its LiteLLM version withheld the models' earlier reasoning without any error, and the resulting losses exceed every difference between the harnesses.

### Effect on the benchmark

```{python}
#| include: false

import json

from scripts.analyze_harness_trials import HARNESS_LABELS, load_trials
from scripts.analyze_reasoning_retention import CHARS_PER_TOKEN, load_rows, reasoning_tokens
from scripts.harness_figures import GRID, HARNESS_COLORS, HARNESS_MARKERS, INK, MUTED

# Trials that lost their earlier reasoning, each paired with the canonical trial of the same
# task and harness that kept it. DeepSeek Claude Code uses the default CLIProxyAPI run (#102),
# which requested `max` effort like the canonical run.
_DATA = Path("data/benchmark-results")
_DS_SUPERSEDED = _DATA / ".superseded/issue-111/deepseek-v4p1-flash"
# The superseded DeepSeek Pi run also holds four trials that kept their reasoning, so DeepSeek
# trials are selected by the retention check. The first GLM run ran entirely before the gateway
# upgrade; five looping Codex trials produced too little reasoning per call to measure, but
# belong to the affected run as well.
LOSS_RUNS = {
    "deepseek": ("deepseek-v4p1-flash",
                 [_DS_SUPERSEDED / "codex", _DS_SUPERSEDED / "pi",
                  _DATA / ".excluded/deepseek-v4p1-flash/claude-code-cliproxy-default"],
                 [_DATA / "deepseek-v4p1-flash"], True),
    "glm": ("glm-5p3-flash", [_DATA / ".excluded/glm-5.3-flash/first-run"], [_DATA / "glm-5.3-flash"], False),
}


def _without_reasoning(model: str, jobs: list[Path], by_retention: bool) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = load_trials(model, jobs)
    if not by_retention:
        return pd.DataFrame(rows)
    lost = {row["trial"] for job in jobs for row in load_rows(job) if row["retained"] is False}
    return pd.DataFrame([row for row in rows if row["trial"] in lost])


_frames = []
for _name, (_model, _without_jobs, _with_jobs, _by_retention) in LOSS_RUNS.items():
    _pairs = _without_reasoning(_model, _without_jobs, _by_retention).merge(
        pd.DataFrame(load_trials(_model, _with_jobs)), on=["task", "harness"],
        suffixes=("_without", "_with"), validate="one_to_one")
    _pairs["model"] = _name
    _frames.append(_pairs)
loss_pairs = pd.concat(_frames, ignore_index=True)
loss_pairs["cost_ratio"] = loss_pairs["cost_usd_without"] / loss_pairs["cost_usd_with"]

_trial_dirs = {path.name: path
               for _, jobs_without, jobs_with, _ in LOSS_RUNS.values()
               for job in jobs_without + jobs_with for path in job.iterdir() if (path / "result.json").exists()}


def _reasoning_output(trial: str) -> int:
    """Reasoning tokens of a trial; estimated from the text where the harness records no counts."""
    steps = [step for step in json.loads((_trial_dirs[trial] / "agent/trajectory.json").read_text())["steps"]
             if step.get("source") == "agent" and step.get("metrics")]
    if any(reasoning_tokens(step) for step in steps):
        return sum(reasoning_tokens(step) or 0 for step in steps)
    return sum(len(step.get("reasoning_content") or "") // CHARS_PER_TOKEN for step in steps)


# Output tokens split into reasoning and visible output (message text and tool calls), per agent step.
for _side in ("without", "with"):
    _reasoning = loss_pairs[f"trial_{_side}"].map(_reasoning_output)
    loss_pairs[f"reasoning_per_step_{_side}"] = _reasoning / loss_pairs[f"agent_steps_{_side}"]
    loss_pairs[f"visible_per_step_{_side}"] = (
        (loss_pairs[f"output_tokens_{_side}"] - _reasoning) / loss_pairs[f"agent_steps_{_side}"])

loss_quoted = {
    m: {
        "pairs": len(g),
        "passed": (int(g["passed_without"].sum()), int(g["passed_with"].sum())),
        "timeouts": (int(g["timeout_without"].sum()), int(g["timeout_with"].sum())),
        "cost": (round(float(g["cost_usd_without"].sum()), 2), round(float(g["cost_usd_with"].sum()), 2)),
        "cost_factor": round(float(g["cost_usd_without"].sum() / g["cost_usd_with"].sum()), 1),
        "cost_per_pass": (round(float(g["cost_usd_without"].sum() / g["passed_without"].sum()), 2),
                          round(float(g["cost_usd_with"].sum() / g["passed_with"].sum()), 2)),
        "cost_per_pass_factor": round(float((g["cost_usd_without"].sum() / g["passed_without"].sum())
                                            / (g["cost_usd_with"].sum() / g["passed_with"].sum())), 1),
        "longest_repeat": int(g["longest_repeat_without"].max()),
        "harness_cost_factor": {h: round(float(x["cost_usd_without"].sum() / x["cost_usd_with"].sum()), 1)
                                for h, x in g.groupby("harness")},
        **{f"{kind}_per_step": {h: tuple(round(float(x[f"{kind}_per_step_{side}"].median()))
                                          for side in ("without", "with"))
                                  for h, x in g.groupby("harness") if h != "claude-code"}
           for kind in ("reasoning", "visible")},
    }
    for m, g in loss_pairs.groupby("model")
}
loss_expected = {
    "deepseek": {"pairs": 21, "passed": (4, 14), "timeouts": (9, 0), "cost": (15.19, 7.82), "cost_factor": 1.9,
                 "cost_per_pass": (3.8, 0.56), "cost_per_pass_factor": 6.8, "longest_repeat": 1,
                 "harness_cost_factor": {"claude-code": 1.9, "codex": 1.9, "pi": 2.1},
                 "reasoning_per_step": {"codex": (4951, 365), "pi": (3844, 669)},
                 "visible_per_step": {"codex": (254, 228), "pi": (220, 238)}},
    "glm": {"pairs": 30, "passed": (2, 19), "timeouts": (9, 1), "cost": (179.07, 29.06), "cost_factor": 6.2,
            "cost_per_pass": (89.54, 1.53), "cost_per_pass_factor": 58.5, "longest_repeat": 1953,
            "harness_cost_factor": {"claude-code": 1.9, "codex": 17.7, "pi": 2.1},
            "reasoning_per_step": {"codex": (3, 150), "pi": (726, 398)},
            "visible_per_step": {"codex": (103, 176), "pi": (193, 260)}},
}
if loss_quoted != loss_expected:
    raise ValueError(f"Reasoning-loss comparison changed; update the text: {loss_quoted}")
```

Two models lost their earlier reasoning in this study: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in parts of its first runs and GLM-5.3-Flash in its complete first run (@sec-gateway-reasoning-history). Both were repeated with the reasoning intact, so every affected trial has a counterpart on the same task and harness (@fig-reasoning-loss-models).

Without its earlier reasoning, each model lost most of the tasks it could otherwise solve, and it did so in every harness. DeepSeek passed 4 of its 21 affected tasks instead of 14, and GLM 2 of its 30 instead of 19. Each call still received the earlier messages and tool results, but not the reasoning that had led to them.

The trials without the earlier reasoning also cost more. DeepSeek's cost rose 1.9-fold, from USD 7.82 to 15.19, and GLM's 6.2-fold, from USD 29.06 to 179.07. Because fewer trials passed at the same time, the cost per passing trial rose far more: from USD 0.56 to 3.80 for DeepSeek, or 6.8 times, and from USD 1.53 to 89.54 for GLM, or 58.5 times.

The two models failed in different ways, which shows once their output tokens are split into reasoning tokens and visible output, the message text and tool calls. DeepSeek kept working without repeating itself, but reasoned far more at every agent step: a median of 4,951 reasoning tokens per step in Codex and 3,844 in Pi, against 365 and 669 with its earlier reasoning. Its visible output per step hardly changed, at 254 and 220 tokens against 228 and 238. It reached the timeout in 9 trials, and its cost rose by about the same factor in every harness. GLM instead fell into loops of identical tool calls (@sec-glm-routes), and in Codex it almost stopped reasoning, with a median of 3 reasoning tokens per step against 150. How far its cost rose depended on the harness. In Pi and Claude Code, it rose 2.1 and 1.9 times, about as much as DeepSeek's. Codex let the loops run for thousands of calls until the timeout, and the cost rose 17.7-fold.

```{python}
#| label: fig-reasoning-loss-models
#| fig-cap: "DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash with and without their earlier reasoning; each trial without it is paired with the trial of the same task and harness with it. (a) Passed trials; the number of affected tasks is given below each harness. (b) Cost of each trial without the earlier reasoning relative to its pair; the dashed line marks equal cost. (c) Longest run of identical consecutive tool calls in each trial without the earlier reasoning. In (b) and (c), filled markers are trials that passed without the earlier reasoning, the bar marks the median, and the axes are logarithmic. The DeepSeek Claude Code trials without earlier reasoning come from the default CLIProxyAPI run, which requested `max` effort."

import numpy as np

_groups = [(m, h) for m in ("deepseek", "glm") for h in ("codex", "pi", "claude-code")]
_positions = [i + (0.7 if m == "glm" else 0) for i, (m, _) in enumerate(_groups)]
_rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
fig, _mosaic = plt.subplot_mosaic([["passed", "passed"], ["cost", "repeat"]], figsize=(6.3, 6.8),
                                   height_ratios=[0.7, 1])
_passed_ax = _mosaic["passed"]
for _x, (_model, _harness) in zip(_positions, _groups, strict=True):
    _g = loss_pairs[(loss_pairs["model"] == _model) & (loss_pairs["harness"] == _harness)]
    _color = HARNESS_COLORS[_harness]
    for _offset, _column, _face in ((-0.19, "passed_with", _color), (0.19, "passed_without", "white")):
        _value = int(_g[_column].sum())
        _passed_ax.bar(_x + _offset, _value, width=0.34, facecolor=_face, edgecolor=_color, linewidth=1.2,
                       zorder=3)
        _passed_ax.text(_x + _offset, _value + 0.15, str(_value), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7,
                        color=INK)
_passed_ax.set_ylim(0, 9.5)
_passed_ax.set_ylabel("(a) Passed trials", fontsize=8)
_passed_ax.legend(handles=[
    plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, facecolor=MUTED, edgecolor=MUTED, label="With earlier reasoning"),
    plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, facecolor="white", edgecolor=MUTED, label="Without earlier reasoning"),
], loc="upper left", fontsize=7, frameon=False)
axes = [_passed_ax, _mosaic["cost"], _mosaic["repeat"]]
for _ax, (_column, _ylabel) in zip(axes[1:], (
    ("cost_ratio", "(b) Relative cost without retained reasoning (retained = 1×)"),
    ("longest_repeat_without", "(c) Longest run of identical tool calls"),
), strict=True):
    for _x, (_model, _harness) in zip(_positions, _groups, strict=True):
        _g = loss_pairs[(loss_pairs["model"] == _model) & (loss_pairs["harness"] == _harness)]
        _color = HARNESS_COLORS[_harness]
        for _value, _passed in zip(_g[_column], _g["passed_without"], strict=True):
            _ax.scatter(_x + _rng.uniform(-0.17, 0.17), _value, s=28, marker=HARNESS_MARKERS[_harness],
                        facecolor=_color if _passed else "white", edgecolor=_color, linewidth=1.2, zorder=3)
        _ax.plot([_x - 0.28, _x + 0.28], [_g[_column].median()] * 2, color=INK, linewidth=2, zorder=4)
    _ax.set_yscale("log")
    _ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda value, _: f"{value:g}"))
    _ax.set_ylabel(_ylabel, fontsize=8)
    _ax.set_xticks(_positions, [HARNESS_LABELS[h] for _, h in _groups], rotation=30, ha="right", fontsize=7.5)
for _ax in axes:
    for _label, _center in (("DeepSeek V4.1 Flash", 1), ("GLM-5.3-Flash", 4.7)):
        _ax.text(_center, 1.02, _label, transform=_ax.get_xaxis_transform(), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8)
    _ax.axvline(2.85, color=GRID, linewidth=1)
    for _side in ("top", "right"):
        _ax.spines[_side].set_visible(False)
    _ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, linewidth=0.8)
    _ax.set_axisbelow(True)
_passed_ax.set_xticks(_positions, [
    f"{HARNESS_LABELS[h]}\n({((loss_pairs['model'] == m) & (loss_pairs['harness'] == h)).sum()} tasks)"
    for m, h in _groups], fontsize=7.5)
axes[1].axhline(1, color=MUTED, linewidth=1, linestyle="--", zorder=2)
fig.tight_layout()
```

The defect was not specific to this benchmark. LiteLLM 1.100.0 added the deletion of `reasoning_content` to its Fireworks provider, and 1.102.0 removed it again [@litellmFireworksStripReasoning; @litellmPr40682]. Every LiteLLM deployment that ran one of these releases and sent thinking models to Fireworks forwarded their requests without the earlier reasoning, for every client and not only for benchmark harnesses. Fireworks accepted the shortened requests, so no client received an error. DeepSeek's own API rejects such requests [@deepseekThinkingMode]; behind the gateway, the missing reasoning turned from an error into silent degradation.

### Cost of the gateway defects

The billed spend of the gateway shows what the defects cost. Every request made with the researcher's gateway user between 2026-08-01 and 2026-09-25 was matched to a trial attempt by model, time, and token counts (@tbl-litellm-spend). Of the USD 816.18 spent on benchmark requests, USD 407.57, half of it, went into runs that the defects made unusable. That is more than the 140 canonical trials cost. The budget these runs consumed also shaped the experiment: Kimi K3 could not be run in OpenCode V2, and GPT-5.6 Luna had to be run through a personal subscription (@sec-methodology). The canonical trials on the gateway were billed USD 288.25, close to their normalized cost of USD 279.99, which supports the cost normalization used in @sec-results.

```{python}

A request belongs to a trial attempt when it used the attempt's model during its run and matches the token counts of one of its steps; unassigned requests fall into the run windows of several attempts with different statuses."

_status = litellm_spend["by_status"]
_deepseek = sum(v for k, v in _status.items()
                if k.startswith(("superseded: deepseek", "excluded: deepseek-v4p1-flash/claude-code-litellm"))
                or k == "overlapping defect-affected attempts")
_spend_rows = [

     _status["excluded: glm-5.3-flash/first-run"] + _status["not published: glm-5.3-flash-2026-09-20"]),

    ("Other benchmark overhead: setup runs, retries, workaround route",
     litellm_spend["by_group"]["other benchmark overhead"]),

    ("Requests outside the benchmark", litellm_spend["by_group"]["outside benchmark"]),
    ("Total", litellm_spend["total_spend_usd"]),
]
Markdown("| Requests | Billed |\n|:--|--:|\n" + "\n".join(
```

### Consequences for AiOrbit users

AiOrbit is the LiteLLM gateway used within IONOS SE (@sec-methodology). It ran LiteLLM 1.101.0 until 2026-09-21 (@sec-gateway-reasoning-history); when it moved to an affected release is not recorded, but the Kimi K3 runs on 2026-09-01 still used 1.98.0. Every AiOrbit user of a Fireworks-served thinking model in that period was therefore affected in the same way as the benchmark. The results above show what such a user would have experienced: a model that solved less than a third of the tasks it solved otherwise, at up to 17.7 times the usual cost in one harness and up to 58.5 times the cost per solved task, with nothing pointing to the gateway. The Claude Code route had a second defect of the same kind: through LiteLLM's Anthropic translation or CLIProxyAPI's default configuration, Claude Code's earlier thinking never reached a non-Anthropic model (@sec-claude-code-reasoning). A gateway is therefore part of the system a user evaluates. Error rates do not reveal such defects, but the prompt-growth check of @sec-gateway-reasoning-history does: it needs only the usage counts that every response already contains.

The defect was a single deleted field in one release of shared infrastructure, and it did not change which models or harnesses were available. It changed only how well they worked. Neither the gateway nor the provider reported it, and a user who first tried one of these models in this period would have had no baseline against which the lower quality stood out. The extent of the damage became measurable only because the same tasks were run again with the reasoning intact and the pass rates, costs, and prompt sizes of both runs could be compared.

AiOrbit is being introduced in stages. A pilot group, which includes the author and later most of the author's team, was invited to replace direct Anthropic API keys with the gateway, and according to the AiOrbit team, the gateway is to become the standard route (personal communication, September 2026). The more usage moves to the gateway, the more users a single defect reaches.

The defects are only partly fixed. The version header of the gateway's responses shows that AiOrbit ran LiteLLM 1.102.1 on 2026-09-24, the version in which the Fireworks defect is fixed. Claude Code's earlier thinking now also reaches the Fireworks models. One step of a Claude Code session was sent through the gateway on 2026-09-25, once with and once without the thinking blocks that the gateway had returned for the previous step. On all three models, the request with them was larger, by about one prompt token per four characters of thinking (@sec-appendix-data). The effort translation is not fixed. A local replay of a Claude Code request with LiteLLM 1.102.1 still forwards `max` as `high`, and AiOrbit still declared no supported effort levels for the three Fireworks models on 2026-09-25 [@pa1Issue94]. Claude Code users of these models therefore still receive less reasoning than they request, without any indication.

Such defects also affect how users judge models. Most survey respondents work with Anthropic models (@fig-survey-provider-diversification), and the gateway offers models of other providers beside them (@sec-methodology). A user who tries one of these models and meets the degraded quality of @fig-reasoning-loss-models has no reason to suspect the gateway and will attribute the result to the model. Defects of this kind therefore work against the adoption of the alternative models the gateway makes available.

## Practical implications

The harness is a decision of its own next to the choice of the model. On the same model and tasks, it moved the result by up to five of ten tasks and the cost by up to a factor of about two, in one combination by more than an order of magnitude. Both effects changed direction from one model to the next, and the largest losses of the study came from the gateway rather than from any harness. For a company that offers several models behind one gateway, this affects both the choice of a harness and the way the whole setup is evaluated.

### Choosing a harness per model

Because no harness was best on every model, the best balance of task success and cost comes from choosing the harness for each model. Where the most solved tasks count, that would have been Claude Code for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, OpenCode V2 for GPT-5.6 Luna, and Codex for Kimi K3; where cost counts as well, OpenCode V2 on all three models it ran on (@fig-cross-cost-success). A user who works with several models therefore benefits from tools that make several harnesses available side by side. Agent orchestration interfaces such as T3 Code and bb control the harnesses installed on a machine, among them Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, from one interface, each on the user's own subscription [@t3code; @bbApp]. With such a tool, using a different harness for a different model does not require a different working environment.

### Choosing one harness

Choosing the best harness per model would require a measurement for every model, including every model added later. For an organization that standardizes on one harness instead, no harness was best for every model, but one was never far behind. OpenCode V2 stayed within one task of the best result on all three of its models (@fig-cross-success), had the lowest cost per passed task on all three (@fig-cross-cost-success), and kept the highest or nearly the highest cache share (@fig-cross-cache), all without working search tools. It is also already the second most used harness in the company (@fig-survey-harness-usage). Claude Code, the most used one, solved the most tasks on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, but it was the most expensive harness on every model it ran, and its delegation multiplied the cost of GPT-5.6 Luna.

Two conditions limit this recommendation. No Claude model was tested, so it does not cover Claude Code in its most common company configuration (@fig-survey-configuration-usage). OpenCode V2 also needs ripgrep installed for its search tools and has to keep its `question` tool out of non-interactive runs, where a question ends the session (@sec-retry-eligibility).

### Evaluation as ongoing work

In a company in which many developers use coding agents, the value of such evaluations grows with the number of users. On the same model and tasks, the harness changed the cost by up to a factor of about two and the number of solved tasks by up to five of ten. For a single user, a small relative difference in cost or success is hardly noticeable. Across a whole company, however, it applies to every task that every user runs. Two thirds of the survey respondents who named an amount spend at least EUR 100 per month on coding agents (@fig-survey-reported-cost). The benchmark requests of this study were billed USD 816.18 (@tbl-litellm-spend), less than ten such users spend in a single month. A choice of model and harness that is only slightly better thus repays an evaluation quickly once it reaches all users. Building and repairing the benchmark setup required considerable further effort and model usage beyond these costs. This effort is spent once and shared by all users, whereas the gains grow with them.

Defects scale in the same way. The gateway defects surfaced only because the same tasks were measured repeatedly with complete trajectories, and in this study alone, the runs they made unusable cost more than all 140 canonical trials (@tbl-litellm-spend). Because the best harness also changed with every model, a result measured once may no longer hold when a model, a harness version, or the gateway changes. Evaluations are therefore most useful as a recurring check. A small fixed task set, rerun after each such change, would reveal regressions before users meet them. Between these runs, the prompt-growth check of @sec-gateway-reasoning-history can watch for lost reasoning continuously, because it needs only the token counts that every response already reports.

## Limitations and threats to validity {#sec-limitations}

The findings rest on single runs of ten tasks per model--harness combination, on the configurations that the budget and the gateway permitted, and on normalized rather than billed costs.

### Sample size and repetition

Every model--harness cell is a single run of ten tasks. According to the minimal-agent reference (@fig-cross-success), a repeated run of the same model can differ by one or two tasks, so smaller differences between harnesses are not interpreted. In this study, eight trials were run twice with the same setup, all on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: four Pi trials of the superseded run that kept their earlier reasoning, and four OpenCode V2 trials that Pier repeated (@sec-retry-eligibility). Two of the eight changed from passed to failed. The GPT-5.6 Luna OpenCode V2 results come from a rerun; the first run compacted at 124,000 instead of 240,000 tokens and passed one task instead of seven (@sec-luna-compaction). This comparison also contains run-to-run variation, and the rerun is used because only its compaction threshold is close to those of the other harnesses.

### Coverage and configuration

The Kimi K3 Claude Code run is excluded, and OpenCode V2 was not run for Kimi K3, so Kimi harness comparisons cover only Pi and Codex (@sec-benchmark-coverage). No Claude model was evaluated. The DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Pi and Claude Code conditions and five of its Codex trials come from repetitions made after the gateway defects had been fixed (@sec-measurement-corrections) [@pa1Issue102; @pa1Issue108; @pa1Issue111]. Codex ran Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash with a profile derived from GPT-5.6 Sol, and OpenCode V2 ran without working search tools (@sec-methodology; @sec-opencode-ripgrep).

The Fireworks-served models ran through a provider whose serving setup is not disclosed. The canonical DeepSeek V4.1 Flash trials span four days because three conditions were repeated after the gateway defects were fixed (@sec-deepseek), and the GLM-5.3-Flash run was repeated completely (@sec-glm-routes). Provider-side changes in this period, such as a different quantization or decoding optimization, would reach the repeated conditions but not the original ones, and the study cannot detect or isolate them. Differences between DeepSeek harnesses that ran on different days may therefore partly reflect the inference setup rather than the harness. The GLM-5.3-Flash results come from a second Fireworks run. The first run lost the earlier reasoning in every trial and is excluded. The comparison of the two runs does not isolate the lost reasoning as the only cause, because the date, the Claude Code route, the context window, and possibly Fireworks' own serving also changed; the second run matches the direct Z.AI batch on the eight tasks both cover (@sec-glm-routes) [@pa1Issue111; @pa1Issue129].

### Measurement

All costs are API-equivalent normalizations of the recorded tokens; the Luna trials were billed through a subscription instead (@sec-cost-accounting). The harnesses count agent steps differently, so step counts are compared only within a model and with care. The cost comparison uses one frozen price list per model; with a different ratio between cached and uncached prices, the cost ranking of the harnesses can change, as the comparison of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash shows. The difficulty weights of @fig-cross-exclusive come from DeepSWE's reference runs across many models and do not describe a task's difficulty for a specific model. The `mini-swe-agent` reference ran on other provider routes than this study, and DeepSWE's public data has changed since the task selection; the rollouts used here are published with the hash of the source file (@sec-appendix-data).
